## Introduction

This tutorial follows Kyle Walker's [An introduction to tidycensus](https://walker-data.com/census-r/an-introduction-to-tidycensus.html) and [Mapping Census data with R](https://walker-data.com/census-r/mapping-census-data-with-r.html) chapters from [Analyzing US Census Data](https://walker-data.com/census-r/). You will pull data from the American Community Survey through the Census API and turn it into one published page with two maps of Texas counties: median household income, and the margin of error that comes with every estimate.

Use AI however you like throughout. An agentic coding tool works best, since it can read and edit your files directly. A chat-based assistant works too, with more copy/paste.

###

The American Community Survey (ACS) is the Census Bureau's rolling annual survey of about 3.5 million households. Unlike the Decennial Census, which counts everyone every ten years, the ACS estimates characteristics like income, education, and age from a sample — which is why every value arrives with a margin of error.

###

[**tidycensus**](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/) returns ACS data as a tidy data frame, one row per geography (or per geography-variable). If you also ask for the geographic boundaries, it hands you an [**sf**](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) object — a table with a spatial column attached — that [**ggplot2**](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) can map directly.

### Exercise 3

Every call to `get_acs()` needs a Census API key. Sign up for a free one at the [Census API key signup page](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html) — the key arrives by email within a few minutes. Click the activation link in that email. The key does not work until you do.

In the R Terminal, run (with your own key in place of `"YOUR-KEY-HERE"`):

```r
tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR-KEY-HERE", install = TRUE)
```

This stores the key in your `.Renviron` file so every future R session finds it automatically. The key is stored on this machine only — on a new machine, install it again with `census_api_key("KEY", install = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)`. In other words, if you install the key in a Codespace, then it disappears when the Codespace does. You will need to do it again when you start a new Codespace, at least until you learn how to create a `dotfiles` repo.

A running R session does not see the new line until it is restarted. Close the R Terminal (the trash icon on its tab) and open a new one, or run `readRenviron("~/.Renviron")`. Then, in the R Terminal, run:

```r
nzchar(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"))
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Sign up for a free Census API key at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html and click the activation link in the email. In the R Terminal, run tidycensus::census_api_key(\"YOUR-KEY-HERE\", install = TRUE) with your own key in place of YOUR-KEY-HERE. Close the R Terminal and open a new one, or run readRenviron(\"~/.Renviron\"). Then, in the R Terminal, run: nzchar(Sys.getenv(\"CENSUS_API_KEY\")) CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
[1] TRUE
```

###

The key is tied to your email, not a Census account, so there is no login to manage. Because `install = TRUE` writes it to `.Renviron` rather than `analysis.qmd`, it never appears in your code or your commits.

## Texas income

Median household income is one of the most-requested ACS variables. Its code is `B19013_001`. In this section you will map it across all 254 Texas counties, and then map how much to trust each county's number.

### Exercise 1

Add a code chunk to `analysis.qmd` that uses **tidycensus** to get 2020 median household income for every county in Texas, with county geometry attached for mapping, and then saves it as `income_tx`. Add `#| message: false` to the chunk to hide the connection messages. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```r
show_file("analysis.qmd")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Add a chunk to analysis.qmd that uses tidycensus to get 2020 median household income for every county in Texas, with county geometry attached for mapping, and saves it as income_tx. Add #| message: false to the chunk to hide the connection messages. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
#| message: false
income_tx <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state = "TX",
  year = 2020,
  geometry = TRUE
)
```

###

Every ACS request comes down to three choices: the **geographic level** (county here, but census tract, place, or state are also available), the **variables** (Census table codes like `B19013_001` for median household income), and the **year**. For the ACS, `year = 2020` retrieves the 2016–2020 5-year estimates, pooled across five years so even small counties have reliable numbers.

###

Every county arrives with a `GEOID` (its FIPS code), a `NAME`, the `variable` code, an `estimate`, and a margin of error (`moe`). The `estimate` is the survey's best guess. The `moe` is the half-width of its 90% confidence interval.

### Exercise 6

Start a new working chunk that summarizes median household income and margin of error across the Texas counties. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```r
show_file("analysis.qmd")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Start a new working chunk that summarizes median household income and margin of error across the Texas counties. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-6-answer
#| echo: true
income_tx |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(
    min_income = min(estimate),
    median_income = median(estimate),
    max_income = max(estimate),
    median_moe = median(moe)
  )
```

###

As always, it is OK if your code/approach differs from ours. The important thing is that you understand what it does and why. Our summary shows the minimum, median, and maximum income across the counties, along with the median margin of error. It is OK if your summary is very different.

Every value in the summary is `NA` because one county, Jeff Davis (GEOID 48243), has no 2020 income estimate: the ACS sample there is too small for the Census Bureau to publish a number. `min()`, `median()`, and `max()` return `NA` whenever a missing value is present, and keep doing so until you add `na.rm = TRUE`.

### Exercise 7

Replace the working chunk with the same summary, dropping the missing county before computing each statistic (`na.rm = TRUE`). Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```r
show_file("analysis.qmd")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with the same summary, dropping the missing county before computing each statistic (na.rm = TRUE). Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-7-answer
#| echo: true
income_tx |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(
    min_income = min(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_income = median(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_income = max(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_moe = median(moe, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

###

Across the 253 counties with an estimate, median household income runs from \$22,716 in Presidio County to \$105,956 in Rockwall County, with a median of \$52,683 and a median margin of error of \$4,486. That one statewide margin hides a lot: the next exercise shows how much it varies from county to county.

### Exercise 8

Replace the working chunk with a table of the ten counties whose margin of error is largest relative to their estimate. Add a column that divides `moe` by `estimate`, sort from largest to smallest, and show `NAME`, `estimate`, `moe`, and the new column. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```r
show_file("analysis.qmd")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with a table of the ten counties whose margin of error is largest relative to their estimate. Add a column that divides moe by estimate, sort from largest to smallest, and show NAME, estimate, moe, and the new column. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-8-answer
#| echo: true
income_tx |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(moe_share = moe / estimate) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_share)) |>
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_share) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

###

Kinney County's estimate is \$39,972, give or take \$26,645, so its 90% interval runs from about \$13,000 to about \$67,000 and says almost nothing. Every county on this list is small: even five pooled years of the survey reach only a few hundred households there. At the other end, Dallas County's margin is \$471 on \$61,870, under 1%. About one Texas county in eight has a margin above 20% of its estimate.

### Exercise 9

Replace the working chunk with a choropleth map of median income across the counties using **ggplot2**. Render and check the map in your Live Server tab.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with a choropleth map of median income across the counties using ggplot2. Render and check the map in your Live Server tab. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-9-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate))
```

###

This is a **choropleth** — each county drawn from its boundary and shaded by its income — and the one county left gray, Jeff Davis in far West Texas, is the missing estimate from the summary. Two things make this first version hard to read: the default blue gradient runs dark-to-light in a direction many readers misjudge, and the gray panel with latitude/longitude gridlines adds clutter a map does not need.

### Exercise 10

Improve the map: give it a perceptually uniform color scale (the [**viridis**](https://sjmgarnier.github.io/viridis/) family is the standard choice), a clear title and legend label, a caption naming the data source, and a clean map theme. Render and compare to ours.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Improve the map: give it a perceptually uniform color scale (the viridis family is the standard choice), a clear title and legend label, a caption naming the data source, and a clean map theme. Render and compare to ours. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-10-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Median income") +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income by county, Texas (2020)",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

###

The **viridis** color scales are perceptually uniform and readable by colorblind viewers, which is why they have become the default for choropleths (the [**RColorBrewer**](https://colorbrewer2.org/) palettes are the other common choice). On the finished map, the highest incomes cluster in the suburban counties around Austin, Dallas–Fort Worth, and Houston, while many rural counties, especially along the Rio Grande border, carry the lowest.

### Exercise 11

Leave the income map in place and start a new working chunk below it that maps the same counties shaded by the margin of error as a share of the estimate (`moe / estimate`). Use the same **viridis** scale and map theme, a legend label, a title, and the source caption. Render.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Leave the income map in place and start a new working chunk below it that maps the same counties shaded by the margin of error as a share of the estimate (moe / estimate). Use the same viridis scale and map theme, a legend label, a title, and the source caption. Render. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-11-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
income_tx |>
  mutate(moe_share = moe / estimate) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = moe_share), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "plasma",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    name = "Margin of error\nas share of estimate"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "How uncertain is each county's median income? Texas (2020)",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

###

The two maps are close to mirror images. The metro counties that carry the highest incomes also have the tightest intervals, because that is where the households are. The sparsely settled counties of West Texas and the border carry both low estimates and the widest intervals, so differences among them are mostly noise. Before you publish a map of an estimate, look at the map of its error.

A choropleth shades each area by a value, so it is only as honest as the variable behind it. Median household income is a good fit because it is roughly comparable across counties. A raw count like "number of high earners" would mostly track county population and mislead.

## Summary

This tutorial followed the **tidycensus** chapters of [Analyzing US Census Data](https://walker-data.com/census-r/) by Kyle Walker. You pulled American Community Survey data through the Census API with **tidycensus**, cached a slow download, learned how ACS estimates carry margins of error, and built one published page with two maps of Texas counties: median household income, and the margin of error as a share of that estimate.

**tidycensus** accepts a state as a name (`"Texas"`), a postal code (`"TX"`), or a FIPS code (`"48"`), and will aggregate to whatever geographic level you ask for — county here, but also census tract, place, or state. The same request scales from a single county map to a national tract-level analysis without changing the approach.

###

The workflow you used here — **tidycensus** to pull ACS data with its boundaries, **sf** to hold the geometry, and **ggplot2** to draw it — is the standard modern approach to US Census analysis. From here, Walker's book goes on to time-series comparisons, spatial statistics, and modeling, all built on the same foundation. The `census-2` tutorial picks up with ACS tables that need no map.
